extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; general public and voters considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political essays arguing that a single, strong national government (union) best secures the safety, defense, commerce, and internal peace of the states, with historical examples and reasoning against division into separate confederacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government reduces just causes of war
rubrics_metrics.description: One general (national) government will give fewer JUST causes of war than several lesser ones because questions are committed to courts appointed by one national government and temptations to swerve from good faith and justice by a governing party of one or two States will be fruitless when reviewed by a national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Independent national courts and laws reduce influence of local interests; temptations from local prospect of loss or advantage have little effect on a national government; example: treaty of peace with Britain adds weight to this reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government better guards against direct unlawful violence
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong united government affords vastly more security against direct and unlawful violences (e.g., Indian hostilities, border provocations) than separate state governments, because such violences are more frequently caused by passions/interests of a part than of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: No Indian war has been occasioned by the (then) federal government but several by individual States; national government is less affected by local circumstances that provoke violence and can more effectively prevent/punish offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government more able to accommodate and settle disputes amicably
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government will be more temperate, cool, moderate, and capable of acting advisedly to accommodate and settle disputes, whereas pride of individual states resists acknowledging and repairing errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: acknowledgments, explanations, and compensations are often accepted from a strong united nation which might be rejected if offered by a small State; historical example: Genoa's humiliation before Louis XIV. shows how a weak polity can be treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union places the country in a posture that does not invite hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety against foreign force depends not only on avoiding just causes of war but on placing and continuing the nation in a situation that does not INVITE hostility or insult — achieved by the best possible state of defense depending on government, arms, and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical elements: efficient government, well-regulated trade, properly organized militia, discreet management of resources and finances, restored credit, and a contented, united people.

rubrics_metrics.name: One government can pool talent, act uniformly, and harmonize policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A single government can collect and avail itself of the talents and experience of the ablest men from across the Union, move on uniform principles of policy, harmonize the parts, and extend foresight and protections to all members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational consequences: unified treaty formation considering whole interests, rapid application of resources to defend any part, uniform militia discipline and a clear line of subordination to central authority to consolidate forces into an efficient corps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unified naval and military capacity requires a single national government
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate governments (or confederacies) would be unable to produce fleets and armies comparable to those of a united nation; only one national government can call forth all national means and materials for forming fleets and consolidated military strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: If England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland had separate governments they would decline into insignificance rather than produce the celebrated fleets of Britain; applied to America, divided states could not raise or pay comparable forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division invites foreign manipulation and conflicting foreign alliances
rubrics_metrics.description: Different confederacies will have distinct commercial concerns, leading to different treaties and degrees of attachment to foreign nations; this divergence makes conflicting foreign alliances likely and invites foreign intrigue and manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: Separate treaties tailored to differing productions/markets create different interests; foreign powers could play confederacies off against one another, and confederacies may seek foreign alliances against each other rather than mutual defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighboring independent nations are naturally hostile without a confederate constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Vicinity or nearness commonly makes nations natural enemies; lacking a confederate constitution that extinguishes secret jealousies, neighboring states are prone to animosity, distrust, and eventual conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited maxims and historical analogies: the experience of divided Britain and other European examples shows how division breeds jealousies and wars; union is presented as the remedy to neighborhood hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic rivalry (commerce/navigation/fisheries) produces inducements to war
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition in fisheries, navigation, carrying trade, and trade to distant markets (China, India) creates real rivalries: our commercial advances will diminish others', provoking jealousies and policies to restrain us, which can become sources or pretexts for hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rivalry with France and Britain in fisheries and navigation; Spain blocking access to Mississippi and Britain to Saint Lawrence demonstrate how commerce-related restrictions create friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce does not guarantee peace — commercial republics can wage war
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument that commerce or the 'genius of republics' will make peaceable neighbors is false in practice: commercial republics and commercial motives have frequently produced as many wars as those of monarchies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical evidence: Athens, Carthage, Rome, Venice, and the Dutch provinces engaged in wars driven at least in part by commercial motives; Britain (commercial) has engaged in many wars influenced by popular/commercial pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human passions and private interests drive nations to conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: National decisions are subject to personal passions, ambition, revenge, and private compacts of rulers or influential individuals; such motives can precipitate wars irrespective of justice or public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/illustrations: Pericles’ actions, the ambitions of ministers like Wolsey, and instances where popular assemblies or favorite leaders pushed nations into war; domestic rebellions (Shays) show danger of internal convulsions spreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into confederacies causes internal dissensions and practical difficulties in mutual defense
rubrics_metrics.description: If the states are split into confederacies, there will be recurring difficulties in coordinating aid, command, proportion of contributions, settlement of peace terms, and dispute arbitration — problems avoided under a single government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational problems enumerated: who commands allied armies, who issues orders, how to apportion aid of men and money, who enforces peace terms — these logistical and diplomatic frictions impede effective defense and compel reliance on a unified authority.
